While Responsible AI principles are widely discussed, less is known about how these principles are translated into concrete mechanisms within Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) and ML production workflows. This paper reports a systematic literature review of studies that operationalize Responsible AI in ML production. The review synthesizes evidence across monitoring and runtime assurance, audit and compliance, ML lifecycle integration, and traceability/provenance/documentation. Across the final study set, the literature shows a shift from abstract ethical principles toward engineering mechanisms such as drift monitoring, runtime checks, audit logs, provenance records, evidence bundles, governance gates, policy-as-code, model passports, and compliance-oriented documentation. However, the evidence base remains uneven: many studies propose architectures or prototypes, while fewer evaluate the mechanisms in realistic production settings, longitudinal operations, or organizational governance workflows. The review identifies a central gap around integrated, evidence-producing Responsible MLOps: current mechanisms often detect, document, or govern isolated parts of the ML lifecycle, but rarely connect runtime signals, ML lifecycle provenance, human accountability, and compliance evidence into closed operational loops. These findings motivate future software engineering research on traceable, evaluable, and operationally integrated Responsible AI support for ML production.

items.title: When Can Self-Play Fix a False Belief? Answer Keys, Pass Bands and Replacement Rules in an Execution-Grounded Loop
items.author: Nirdesh Chauhan, Dushyant Rajput, Siddharth Kosaraju
items.content: Self-play loops in which a model writes tasks, derives an answer key and trains on its own matching solutions are often called grounded when the key comes from executing code. We ask which false beliefs such a loop removes. We run expert-iteration self-play with Qwen3-4B-Base on output-prediction tasks, vary the source of the answer key, and track natural beliefs about Python semantics and two misreadings of task specifications planted by fine-tuning ("at most n" read as < n; "the k-th smallest" read as 0-indexed). Executing the generator's own code gave a key that encoded the "at most" misreading on every audited task, and training on it never raised the truth rate above 0.03. A key from an implementation by the unplanted model, a teacher without the error, raised it to 0.23-0.58 after three rounds in four runs. A correct key is not sufficient: the pass band, which keeps tasks solved 1-7 times of 8, admits almost no corrective task while a belief is held on nearly every sample. Execution keys sharply reduced both natural runtime beliefs on diagnostic items in both seeds. Corrections came with replacement rules that fail on neighbouring items the old belief got right. The robust case, present in all four spec runs, is that after the "at most" fix the model increasingly counts the nearest value above a limit that is absent from the list (overcount 0.18-0.38 of control samples at round 3), a case our planted generators almost never wrote (4 of 10,924 tasks); diagnostic-only metrics miss it. Asked for those cases, the planted generator wrote none in 2,061 checkable tasks, against 27% for the untrained unplanted model in one round. Both generators often moved the request into the specification instead ("the cap itself does not count"), and a decorrelated key follows the specification.

items.title: Call-Level Revision Contracts for LLM-Authored Workflows
items.author: Chenyang Jiang, Benyang Pan, Puqu Wu
items.content: Durable execution engines replay a recorded history and do not compare activity payloads. When a model repairs a workflow that failed partway through, it must either pay again for calls that succeeded or accept a recorded result whose payload changed. We define a revision contract for workflows whose orchestration code is written by a model. Each capability call carries a structural identity built from its callsite, its fanout position, and its occurrence count, and the identity stays stable under rewrites that leave the call in place, so committed identities form a frozen prefix. The frozen unit is the call expression, and the surrounding code stays writable. A static gate rejects a rewrite that would change a committed call before a container starts. A runtime digest stops a changed payload at a committed identity, and an occurrence ledger names a repeated paid payload. Under three assumptions, a candidate the gate accepts replays every committed call it invokes, executes only new work, and reports the identities it skips. No local identity is both relocation-invariant and free of wrong reuse, so callsite identity turns a relocation into a pre-spend stop. On media workflows, 22 gate-passed repairs replay 258 committed identities with no duplicate, and a live six-way fanout makes seven paid calls instead of twelve. A 12-task customer-support study applies the same identity, replay, and boundary checks on two models.

items.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Verifying Diagnostic Signal Reachability in Electronic Systems
items.author: Heba Jaradat, Mohammed-Khalil Ghali, Saurabh Kulkarni, Rohan Kulkarni, Sangwon Yoon
items.content: Diagnostic Signal Reachability (DSR) captures whether board-level health signals are observable by management controllers, including baseboard management controllers (BMCs), complex programmable logic devices (CPLDs), and other smart controllers. Verifying DSR is essential for field diagnosability in datacenter fleets, where one design is deployed at massive scale, yet it remains largely manual, since each signal is traced by hand across schematic sheets, renamed nets, series components, and monitoring devices. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive but unreliable at structural connectivity reasoning, where over-claiming can silently hide a rare coverage gap. We present NetFlow-DSR, a neuro-symbolic framework in which an LLM orchestrates the DSR pipeline and resolves device roles mainly from part-name families and library pin names, consulting specifications only for ambiguous parts. Pin directionality is read from the design library, and deterministic graph engines verify connectivity over the authoritative netlist. The pipeline detects diagnostic nets, canonicalizes renamed net fragments, and performs controller-seeded, power-aware breadth-first search over an admissibility graph that credits device-mediated monitoring. Each verdict carries an auditable trace card whose proof path is the witness. Across five production boards from an AI platform, covering 421 expert-graded signals, a three-stage ablation improves pooled F1 from 0.578 to 0.944. Because a monitored verdict is emitted only with a proof path, the verifier is sound by construction, and precision and specificity were 100% in the evaluated data. In a cross-model study on the system-controller module, precision remained 100% across three LLMs while recall tracked each model's device-semantic extraction. Precision therefore depends on the netlist-grounded verifier and correct device semantics rather than on any single LLM.

items.title: DMuon: Scaling Matrix Optimizers in Data Parallelism with Topology-Aware Matrix Ownership and Communication
items.author: Starrick Liu, Ruizhi Chengze, Lufang Chen, Michael Zhao, Ran Yu, Xiaofan Li, dance kuzi, Yue Zhang, Zijuan Lin, SongAo Han, YongHua Chen, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang
items.content: Matrix optimizers such as Muon update whole weight matrices, which conflicts with the element- or row-wise sharding of data-parallel runtimes. Once parameters are sharded as well, matrix optimizers incur extra communication or repeated computation. We present DMuon, a matrix-granular optimizer runtime for PyTorch FSDP (ZeRO-2/3) and HSDP. DMuon assigns each matrix a unique owner, which performs the Newton--Schulz (NS) iteration and optimizer update on the full matrix, and balances the load across owners by computational cost. On HSDP, ownership is global across replicas, so the cluster keeps a single copy of gradients and optimizer state, and updated parameters are published across nodes as soon as they are ready, overlapping subsequent computation. This layout makes every collective sparse and variable in length, so DMuon schedules these collectives as their data becomes ready and routes them along the cluster's two-level network. On up to 256 H100 GPUs, across three dense LLMs and two VLA models, DMuon matches or exceeds the training throughput of PyTorch FSDP2 with AdamW, reaching 1.05$\times$ that of FSDP2 with AdamW at the median on 256 GPUs. The optimized parameter gathering and gradient reduction absorb the extra communication and computation a matrix optimizer requires. Against a gather-then-replicate Muon baseline, DMuon's throughput is 2.1 times as high at the median.

items.title: NUMA-Torch: Compiler-Driven NUMA-Aware LLM Prefill on Multi-Socket CPUs
items.author: Thisara Rathnayaka Weerakoon (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Ishan Dewpura (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Niman Ransindu (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Shavin Anjitha (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka), Tharindu R. Patabandi (Independent Researcher, San Jose, CA, USA), Sanath Jayasena (Department of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka)
items.content: For sufficiently large transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), whose parameters cannot be retained in on-chip caches, prefill throughput on multi-socket CPUs is often limited by sustainable DRAM bandwidth rather than peak floating-point throughput. In the standard PyTorch compilation (i.e., TorchInductor) path, model weights are allocated without considering the Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) topology: specifically, the affinity between memory banks and compute cores is disregarded. This causes a substantial fraction of weight accesses to traverse the inter-socket interconnect, severely degrading the effective memory bandwidth available to each socket. We address this bottleneck through a compiler-level solution that makes TorchInductor NUMA-aware. Treating each NUMA socket as an independent tensor-parallel partition, we introduce NUMA-aware Tensor Parallelism (NUMA-TP). This approach transparently shards weights across sockets and schedules compute kernels such that thread pools and memory allocations remain strictly local to their respective sockets using CPU affinity. We evaluate the approach on GPT-2 (117M, 345M, 762M) and BERT (Small, Large), which exercise standard multi-head attention and MLP, as well as Gemma 3 270M, which combines Multi-Query Attention with a GeGLU-gated MLP. By strictly enforcing data locality, our approach successfully mitigates cross-socket traffic, achieving prefill speedups of up to 2.63x on a dual-socket Haswell platform, up to 1.87x on a dual-socket Cascade Lake platform, and up to 2.27x on a four-socket Haswell-EX platform.

items.title: Automatic Assistance to Reduce Information Overload during Software Issue Report Understanding
items.author: Salma Begum Tamanna, Gias Uddin, Junaed Younus Khan, Lan Xia, Longyu Zhang
items.content: Modern issue tracking systems are used to log an issue and track it from its inception to closure. Issue reports with diverse discussions from stakeholders can be large and verbose, making them challenging to analyze quickly. Our developer interviews revealed that they struggled with the diverse information in issue reports and demanded automated techniques to classify and summarize information. We designed a tool, iSum (issue summarizer), that helps with the automatic classification and summarization of information types discussed in issue reports. The summarizer offers two views: 1. Developer View takes an issue report as input and outputs visualized summaries of information in the report. 2. Manager View takes a suite of all issue reports under a given software project as inputs and shows the prevalence and trends of different information types across the reports. We evaluated iSum through three studies. 1. In an empirical study over two benchmarks, iSum offers, on average, 11-13% higher F1-scores than state-of-the-art baselines to detect information types. 2. We conducted a user study in task-based setup with 30 developers to determine iSum's effectiveness in issue exploration scenarios. Results showed increased productivity and accuracy with iSum compared to manual inspection. 3. We assessed iSum's feasibility for development and management tasks. It proved useful to both developers and project managers for issue comprehension and trend monitoring.

items.title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
items.author: Yichao Fu, Yuxuan Zhang, Minshen Zhang, Ruitian Wang, Junda Chen, Hao Zhang
items.content: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and tune FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting. Experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only profiles of colocated vLLM, telling whether switching to AFD would pay off before deploying it. The model yields a concise insight: AFD's speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to 2.48x with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/FastAFD.

items.title: Beyond Proof of Possession: A Relational Theory of Authority
items.author: Nicola Gallo
items.content: Proof-of-Possession (PoP) establishes that an executor controls an artifact (key, token, credential, or capability), but such control alone determines neither the executor's relational profile nor the causal history of an execution occurrence. We separate PoP from Proof of Relationship (PoR), the semantic property that one execution occurrence validly continues another, and from authorization, which is occurrence-sensitive. The foundational change is in the semantic domain of authorization: from holders and authority-bearing artifacts to execution occurrences situated in causal histories. We give authorization models an observation-based occurrence verdict and a separate transition-admissibility relation; kernel inclusion yields a partial order on observation-kernel classes. Building on Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) and Proof-of-Continuity (PoC), we classify executors by authorization-relevant equivalence relations whose quotients form relational profile spaces, with positive predicates over profile transitions forming a distributive lattice. This adds relational attenuation to authority attenuation: along a valid causal history, $C_{i+1}\subseteq C_i$ and $\rho_{i+1}\Rightarrow\rho_i$. We prove dual monotonicity, combined closure, and origin relational closure. Two occurrences of the same authenticated executor, with the same profile and possession evidence, need not be authorization-equivalent, and within a valid PIC lineage a deputy's independent authority cannot be imported outside the origin context. Finally, we prove that the executor-dependent decision factors through the relational profile and is invariant under sound mechanisms establishing it: successor-side PoP is a possible evidence mechanism, not a necessary premise of authorization. Under explicit Witness Assumptions, a boundary-witnessed checkpoint construction realizes the premises without successor-side PoP.

items.title: Full Provenance on the COSS Causal Axis: An Event-Level Closure of Causal Attribution and Confused-Deputy Exclusion
items.author: Nicola Gallo
items.content: Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) represents an authority-use event as an operation/resource behavior situated in a causal lineage, $(o,r,\ell)\in O\times R\times L$. We make the causal occurrence itself primitive: a represented security-relevant causal graph $(E,\to_c)$ in which each occurrence has a unique causal history, so the consistent event-lineage space is canonically isomorphic to $E$. The modeled execution has one causal partial order; distinct lineages are distinct causal histories inside it and may share a root while diverging into incomparable branches. PIC's $O\times R\times L$ is the authority-behavior projection of this space, and Causally Ordered Security-State (COSS) continuity generalizes it to an arbitrary behavior product over the same causal execution. On this semantics we prove an architecture-independent confused-deputy exclusion theorem. PIC continuation requires $C(e')\subseteq C(e)$ on every ordinary causal edge, so descendants are bounded by their ancestors; at an ordinary join, authority available on only one incoming branch cannot be resurrected, even when branches share a common root. Non-conservative combination must be an explicit authorized composition or relaxation event. With protected-effect mediation, an effect caused by request $q$ through an ordinary authority segment can exercise only authority in $C(q)$, so a confused-deputy state is contradictory. The result holds for any system whose protected request-to-effect causes are faithfully represented and whose ordinary authority transport satisfies PIC. We revisit Rajani, Garg, and Rezk: their value, control-flow, and initial-heap attacks are different witnesses of causal ancestry, so full provenance is an evidence mechanism for recovering edges of the causal graph, not the foundation of the PIC theorem. Finally we lift it to the COSS product of heterogeneous security-state coordinates.

items.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
items.author: Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, Zihao Lin
items.content: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.

items.title: Global Surveillance Under the Lens: Reconstructing Passive Dolev-Yao Intruders
items.author: Paolo Modesti
items.content: Global surveillance systems record large volumes of network traffic for retrospective analysis, but packet captures alone reveal little about protocol-level semantics. This paper presents an automated, specification-guided methodology for reconstructing passive Dolev-Yao intruder executions from captured network traffic and validating the reconstructed executions against a formal protocol specification. The framework takes a PCAP capture, an AnBx specification, and the associated deployment metadata; it extracts Java-serialised objects from TCP streams, reconstructs protocol sessions and channel-to-step assignments, and generates a passive intruder that evaluates the Dolev-Yao derived checks produced by the AnBx compiler. Three reconstruction challenges are addressed: multiple serialised objects and object references within a TCP stream, ambiguity in mapping interleaved connections to concurrent protocol sessions, and semantic validation of candidate reconstructions. We evaluate the methodology on 121 protocols from the AnBx test suite. For single-session captures, the standard JDK cryptographic provider recovers 97.8% of expected objects and achieves 94.2% successful reconstruction, where success requires complete object recovery and a clean passive-intruder execution. For the 112 parallel-capable protocols, the toolchain achieves 89.3% successful reconstruction for both two and three concurrent sessions, while recovering approximately 97.2% of expected objects. Experiments with mismatched protocol-role mappings and deliberately mutated traces show that the generated Dolev-Yao checks respond to semantic inconsistencies. By making the reconstruction step explicit, the solution produces protocol-level observations on which assessments of protocol resilience and the design of defensive countermeasures can be built.

items.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
items.author: \'Alvaro F. Silva, Martim Afonso, Nuno Saavedra, Emily First, Alexandra Mendes, Jo\~ao F. Ferreira
items.content: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.

items.title: Capability Gain from ISA to Shared Execution on AMD MI300A and MI250X
items.author: Aaron Jarmusch, Sunita Chandrasekaran
items.content: Each new GPU generation is showcased by its peak instruction rates, yet users hardly ever run instructions directly: they reach the hardware's performance through vendor libraries, applications and devices shared with other jobs. How much of a theoretical speedup survives these layers is rarely measured, so a team deciding whether to move to a new generation, or to adopt FP8 or 2:4 sparsity, lacks adequate guidance. AMD's MI300A (CDNA3) adds new FP8 matrix instructions and 2:4 structured-sparse instructions that the predecessor, the MI250X (CDNA2), does not have. We analyze this theoretical speedup gap on AMD's MI300A (CDNA3) against the MI250X (CDNA2) by defining a new metric, capability gain. Capability gain is the fraction of a feature's instruction-level speedup that it keeps at a higher level, such as a library, an application or a shared device. We trace it from ISA microbenchmarks through hipBLASLt and hipSPARSELt to LLM inference and mixed-precision HPL, and onto a device shared by up to eight concurrent streams. FP8 keeps most of its speedup through the library, completing an $8192^3$ GEMM \genCapPkgEndToEndGainEightK{} faster than the MI250X with FP16, but unfused quantization turns it into a per-layer slowdown in an LLM, and 2:4 sparsity keeps at most about half of its speedup in hipSPARSELt. Under queue sharing, FP8's GEMM capability gain rises above 1. How fairly streams share the device depends on the number of hardware queues, not on the numeric precision, yet shared LLM serving gains nothing from FP8.

items.title: Not All Loops Cost the Same: Phase-Dependent Depth for Serving Looped Transformers
items.author: Zhixu Du, Yuhan Cheng, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
items.content: Looped transformers scale inference-time reasoning by repeatedly reusing a shared core, increasing computation without increasing parameter count. Serving prefilling and decoding with a uniform loop budget couples their costs. We present LoopDuet, a phase-dependent depth and training-free serving approach that selects the two budgets jointly while preserving decoding depth at prefilling boundaries. Our vLLM implementation gathers tokens requiring further recurrence into compact batches, turning the selected allocation into executable savings with existing weights and attention kernels. At runtime, a queue-age controller adjusts prefilling depth to retain quality as demand changes. Experiments on the full HotpotQA dataset with one A100-80GB demonstrate two benefits of this flexibility. First, separate phase budgets improve the quality--throughput trade-off: Huginn delivers 19\% more throughput than the fastest tested uniform setting meeting the same accuracy criterion, while a higher-throughput operating point gains 6.04 EM points over uniform depth eight at 97\% of its throughput. Second, the same execution mechanism retains more quality under load: on two evaluated OLMo arrival traces, adaptive prefilling gains 0.92--1.35 EM points over the most accurate tested fixed-depth controls at the same 100\% attainment of a one-second time-to-first-token target. Together, these results establish LoopDuet as a practical way to turn flexible model computation into higher serving capacity and better quality under load.

items.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
items.author: Woosang Lim (SAINT Machines, KAIST), Yeseul Chang (Chung-Ang University), Jaewoo Lee (Chung-Ang University)
items.content: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

items.title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
items.author: Melika Sepidband, Jiho Shin, Song Wang, Hadi Hemmati
items.content: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency. In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench. The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring. On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.

items.title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
items.author: Dingxian Wang, Zhe Fu, Jiaqi Deng, Chao Yin, Ganesh Prabhu, Karthik Gomadam Rajagopal, Darwin Yi, Huan Huo, Guandong Xu, Xianzhi Wang, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen
items.content: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.
